title: Dido ad templum. Ilioneus orat
titleEn: Dido at the Temple; Ilioneus Pleads — Aeneid I.466–560
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas, still gazing at the pictures on the temple wall, finds more of the Trojan War there: the Greeks and Trojans driving each other back and forth around Pergamum, the tents of Rhesus betrayed in sleep and Diomedes driving off his horses, the boy Troilus dragged behind his chariot with his hair in the dust, the Trojan women bringing a robe to an unfriendly Pallas, Hector dragged round the walls and sold for gold to Priam, and Aeneas himself among the Greek leaders, with Memnon's eastern troops and the Amazon queen Penthesilea, a bared breast above her golden belt. While he stands rapt, Dido arrives, as beautiful as Diana leading her dance on the Eurotas, and takes her seat at the temple doors to give judgment and share out the work. Suddenly Aeneas sees his lost companions Antheus, Sergestus and Cloanthus coming in with a crowd. He and Achates are glad and afraid; hidden in their cloud, they hold back to learn how the others fare. The envoys are admitted and Ilioneus, the oldest of them, speaks: they are wretched Trojans blown over every sea, who ask the queen to keep fire from their ships and to look kindly on a pious people; they have come to Libya neither to plunder nor to raid, but were bound for Italy when the storm drove them off course. What sort of people forbids even a landing on the beach? If she scorns men, let her still fear gods who mark right and wrong. Their king Aeneas was the justest and bravest of men; if he lives, she will not regret being first in kindness; if he is lost, they ask only leave to repair the fleet and sail on to Sicily and King Acestes. All the Trojans murmur their assent.
part: Dido at the Temple; Ilioneus Pleads (I.466–560)

sentences.t:
Namque videbat, uti bellantes Pergama circum
hac fugerent Graii, premeret Troiana iuventus,
hac Phryges, instaret curru cristatus Achilles.
sentences.l:
For he saw, how, fighting around Pergamum,
on this side the Greeks fled, the Trojan youth pressed on,
on that side the Phrygians, crested Achilles bore down in his chariot.
sentences.i: For he saw how, in the fighting around Pergamum, the Greeks were fleeing on one side with the Trojan youth pressing them, and on the other the Phrygians, with plumed Achilles bearing down upon them in his chariot.
sentences.n: The pictures on Juno's temple wall go on (I.456 ff.). 'Namque' explains why he is weeping. 'uti ... fugerent ... premeret ... instaret' — 'uti' (= 'ut') with the imperfect subjunctive in an indirect question after 'videbat': how the Greeks were fleeing. 'hac ... hac' — 'on this side ... on that'. 'Graii' (from 'Graius') is the poets' word for the Greeks, beside the prose 'Graeci'; 'Phryges' (Phrygians) is a poets' name for the Trojans. 'cristatus' — crested, plumed (of the helmet). The whole passage is an ecphrasis, a description of a work of art, in the manner of the Shield of Achilles (Iliad 18); here the art shows Aeneas his own war from outside.

sentences.t:
Nec procul hinc Rhesi niveis tentoria velis
adgnoscit lacrimans, primo quae prodita somno
Tydides multa vastabat caede cruentus,
ardentisque avertit equos in castra, prius quam
pabula gustassent Troiae Xanthumque bibissent.
sentences.l:
Not far from here the tents of Rhesus with snowy canvas
he recognises, weeping, which, betrayed in first sleep,
the son of Tydeus was laying waste, bloody with much slaughter,
and he drives off the fiery horses into the camp, before
they could taste the fodder of Troy and drink the Xanthus.
sentences.i: Not far from there he recognises, weeping, the tents of Rhesus with their snow-white canvas. Betrayed in their first sleep, they were being laid waste by Diomedes, red with heavy slaughter; and he drives the fiery horses off to the Greek camp, before they could taste Trojan grass or drink the Xanthus.
sentences.n: The Rhesus episode of Iliad 10 (the 'Doloneia'): Diomedes ('Tydides', 'son of Tydeus', a Greek patronymic) and Odysseus killed the Thracian king Rhesus in his sleep and took his famous white horses. A later story, not in Homer, said that if those horses grazed on Trojan grass and drank the river Xanthus, Troy could never fall; hence 'prius quam' with the subjunctive of an act forestalled, 'before they could taste ... and drink'. 'gustassent' is the contracted pluperfect subjunctive for 'gustavissent'; 'bibissent' is the regular pluperfect subjunctive of 'bibo'. 'Rhesi' — genitive of 'Rhesus'. 'adgnoscit' — Greenough's spelling of 'agnoscit', 'recognises', a historical present. 'ardentis ... equos' — accusative plural in -is. 'avertit' may be present or perfect, the spelling being the same.

sentences.t:
Parte alia fugiens amissis Troilus armis,
infelix puer atque impar congressus Achilli,
fertur equis, curruque haeret resupinus inani,
lora tenens tamen;
sentences.l:
In another part, Troilus fleeing, his arms lost,
unlucky boy and an unequal match meeting Achilles,
is carried by his horses, and clings on, on his back, to the empty chariot,
holding the reins nevertheless;
sentences.i: In another part Troilus is fleeing with his weapons lost, an unlucky boy and no match for Achilles. His horses bear him along and he clings flat on his back to the empty chariot, still holding the reins;
sentences.n: Troilus, a young son of Priam, was ambushed and killed by Achilles. Homer only names him among Priam's dead sons (Iliad 24.257); the story was told in the lost epic Cypria and was a favourite subject of Greek vase-painters. 'amissis armis' is ablative absolute; 'impar ... congressus' — 'unequal, having met (him) in combat' (perfect participle of the deponent 'congredior', here with the dative 'Achilli'); 'Achilli' — dative of 'Achilles'. 'fertur equis' — 'is carried by his horses'; 'curru ... inani' — dative or ablative with 'haeret' ('clings to the empty chariot': the car has no driver). 'resupinus' — lying on his back. 'lora tenens tamen' — 'holding the reins nonetheless': the pathos is that he never lets go.

sentences.t:
huic cervixque comaeque trahuntur
per terram, et versa pulvis inscribitur hasta.
sentences.l:
for him both neck and hair are dragged
along the ground, and the dust is written upon by the turned spear.
sentences.i: his neck and hair trail along the ground, and the dust is scored by his reversed spear.
sentences.n: 'huic ... trahuntur' — dative of the person affected, 'for him', in effect 'his neck and hair are dragged'. 'cervixque comaeque' — the double '-que ... -que', 'both neck and hair'. 'versa ... hasta' — ablative: the spear is turned round and trails a line in the dust; 'inscribitur' — the dust 'is written upon'. A cruelly exact detail.

sentences.i: Meanwhile the women of Troy, with their hair unbound, were going to the temple of unfriendly Pallas, carrying a robe, sad and pleading, beating their breasts with their palms;
sentences.n: A scene from Iliad 6, where Hecuba and the Trojan women take a robe (the 'peplum') to Athena's temple and pray her to break Diomedes' spear and pity the city; she refuses. 'Palladis' is the genitive of 'Pallas'. 'non aequae' — 'not even-handed', hence unkind. 'Iliades' — a Greek form: 'women of Ilium'. 'suppliciter' — adverb, 'in the manner of suppliants', with 'tristes'. 'crinibus ... passis' — ablative absolute, with the participle of 'pando' (loosened, spread) — a sign of mourning or entreaty. 'tunsae pectora palmis' — 'beaten as to their breasts' (accusative of respect with a passive participle: a Greek-style construction common in Virgil). 'ibant' — the imperfect, scene still in progress.

sentences.t: diva solo fixos oculos aversa tenebat.
sentences.l: the goddess, turned away, held her eyes fixed on the ground.
sentences.i: the goddess, turned from them, kept her eyes fixed on the ground.
sentences.n: 'diva ... aversa' — Pallas, turned away. 'solo fixos oculos' — her eyes fixed on the ground: the refusal of the Iliad scene is made visible. Note the line's order: 'diva' first, 'tenebat' last, and the whole gesture between.

sentences.t:
Ter circum Iliacos raptaverat Hectora muros,
exanimumque auro corpus vendebat Achilles.
sentences.l:
Three times around the Trojan walls he had dragged Hector,
and Achilles was selling the lifeless body for gold.
sentences.i: Three times he had dragged Hector around the walls of Ilium, and Achilles was selling the lifeless body for gold.
sentences.n: Two scenes are put side by side. In Homer Achilles chases the living Hector three times round the walls and drags the body to the ships (Iliad 22), later three times round Patroclus' tomb, and Priam ransoms it (Iliad 24); the dragging round the walls is a later version of the story. 'Hectora' — Greek accusative (-a). 'raptaverat' — 'had dragged to and fro' (a frequentative: 'rapto'), pluperfect, so the dragging is over before the selling. 'exanimum ... corpus' — 'lifeless body'; the 'auro' is the ransom Priam brought. Nothing in this scene is merely told; each detail is chosen to be the one that hurts Aeneas.

sentences.t:
Tum vero ingentem gemitum dat pectore ab imo,
ut spolia, ut currus, utque ipsum corpus amici,
tendentemque manus Priamum conspexit inermis.
sentences.l:
Then indeed he gives a great groan from the bottom of his breast,
when the spoils, when the chariot, and when the very body of his friend,
and Priam stretching out unarmed hands, he beheld.
sentences.i: Then indeed he gives a great groan from the depths of his heart, as he sees the spoils, the chariot, the very body of his friend, and Priam stretching out unarmed hands.
sentences.n: 'Tum vero' — 'then indeed', the point at which a feeling overflows. 'pectore ab imo' — 'from the lowest part of the chest', the deepest part. 'ut ... ut ... utque' — temporal 'ut', 'when', repeated before each object of the one verb 'conspexit' (perfect): the spoils, the chariot, the body of 'amici' ('friend': Hector). The last object, Priam stretching out his hands, is the climax. 'inermis' is accusative plural (in -is) agreeing with 'manus' (feminine): 'unarmed hands'.

sentences.t:
Se quoque principibus permixtum adgnovit Achivis,
Eoasque acies et nigri Memnonis arma.
sentences.l:
He recognised himself too mixed in with the Achaean chiefs,
and the eastern lines and the arms of black Memnon.
sentences.i: He recognised himself, too, mingled with the Greek chiefs, and the eastern ranks and the arms of dark Memnon.
sentences.n: 'Se quoque ... adgnovit' — Aeneas sees himself in the picture, fighting among the Greek princes (in the Iliad he did fight Achilles, Iliad 20). 'Achivis' — the Achaeans, another name for the Greeks. 'permixtum' — 'mingled, in the thick of'. 'Eoas acies' — the lines from the East ('Eos' = Dawn, whence the adjective). Memnon, king of the Ethiopians and son of Dawn, came to help Troy after Hector's death and was killed by Achilles; Homer only names him (Odyssey 4.188, 11.522), and his story was told in the lost epic Aethiopis. 'Eoas' has three syllables, E-o-as. 'nigri' — dark-skinned.

sentences.t:
Ducit Amazonidum lunatis agmina peltis
Penthesilea furens, mediisque in milibus ardet,
aurea subnectens exsertae cingula mammae,
bellatrix, audetque viris concurrere virgo.
sentences.l:
There leads the Amazons' columns with their crescent shields
Penthesilea, raging, and in the midst of thousands she blazes,
binding golden belts under her bared breast,
a warrior-woman, and the maiden dares to clash with men.
sentences.i: Penthesilea leads the Amazon columns with their crescent shields, wild with fury, and blazes in the midst of the thousands, binding a golden girdle below her bared breast: a warrior woman, a maiden daring to meet men in battle.
sentences.n: Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, came to Troy after Hector's death and was killed by Achilles (told, like Memnon's story, in the Aethiopis). 'Amazonidum' — genitive plural of 'Amazonis' (-idis), a third-declension Greek noun, so the -um is the regular ending. 'lunatis ... peltis' — 'with crescent-shaped light shields' (ablative of description); the 'pelta' was the Amazon's shield. 'furens' — raging. 'Penthesilea' has five syllables, Pen-the-si-le-a. 'aurea subnectens exsertae cingula mammae' — 'fastening golden belts below her bared breast': 'mammae' is dative with the compound 'subnectens' ('binding under'), and 'cingula' is a poetic plural for one belt; the bared breast is the Amazon mark. 'bellatrix' — 'woman-warrior', a feminine noun. 'audetque viris concurrere virgo' — the line ends on 'virgo', 'maiden', in sharp contrast to 'viris'. Virgil is preparing Dido, another woman who leads, who walks in next.

sentences.t:
Haec dum Dardanio Aeneae miranda videntur,
dum stupet, obtutuque haeret defixus in uno,
regina ad templum, forma pulcherrima Dido,
incessit magna iuvenum stipante caterva.
sentences.l:
While these things seem to Dardanian Aeneas wonders to behold,
while he stands stunned and clings fixed in one gaze,
the queen to the temple, most beautiful in form, Dido,
advanced, with a great crowd of young men thronging about her.
sentences.i: While Aeneas the Trojan was marvelling at these things, while he stood amazed, fixed in one unbroken gaze, the queen, Dido, most beautiful of women, came in state to the temple with a great crowd of young men thronging round her.
sentences.n: A new paragraph and a new character. 'Haec dum ... videntur, dum stupet ... haeret' — 'dum', 'while', takes the present indicative even though the main verb ('incessit', perfect) is past: the regular Latin idiom. 'Dardanio' — Dardanian, i.e. Trojan (Dardanus was the ancestor of the Trojan kings). 'miranda' — a gerundive, 'to be wondered at'; 'Aeneae' is dative with 'videntur', 'seem to Aeneas'. 'obtutu ... in uno' — 'in one fixed look'. 'forma pulcherrima Dido' — Dido appears in person for the first time (Venus described her story at I.340–368); 'forma' is ablative of respect. 'incessit' — from 'incedo', to advance with a stately step. 'magna iuvenum stipante caterva' — ablative absolute, 'a great band of young men crowding round', so her entry is staged as a procession.

sentences.t:
Qualis in Eurotae ripis aut per iuga Cynthi
exercet Diana choros, quam mille secutae
hinc atque hinc glomerantur oreades; illa pharetram
fert umero, gradiensque deas supereminet omnis:
sentences.l:
Such as on the banks of Eurotas or along the ridges of Cynthus
Diana plies her dances, whom, following, a thousand
on this side and that throng together, the mountain-nymphs; she a quiver
bears on her shoulder, and as she goes she towers above all the goddesses:
sentences.i: Like Diana, when she leads her dances on the banks of the Eurotas or along the ridges of Cynthus, and a thousand mountain nymphs who follow her crowd about her on every side; she carries her quiver on her shoulder, and as she walks she stands above all the goddesses:
sentences.n: The simile begins: 'Qualis ... talis erat Dido' (503) — 'such as ... such was Dido'. It is modelled on the Odyssey 6.102–109, where Nausicaa among her maids is compared to Artemis on Taygetus; for Homer's Taygetus and Erymanthus Virgil has the Eurotas (Sparta's river) and Cynthus (the mountain on Delos where Diana and Apollo were born). 'quam ... secutae' — 'whom, having followed' (the participle of the deponent 'sequor', agreeing with 'oreades'). 'oreades' — Greek: nymphs of the mountains; four syllables, o-re-a-des. 'Diana' here has a long first syllable (the poets use both quantities). 'hinc atque hinc' — 'from this side and from that'. 'deas ... omnis' — accusative plural in -is.

sentences.t:
Latonae tacitum pertemptant gaudia pectus:
talis erat Dido, talem se laeta ferebat
per medios, instans operi regnisque futuris.
sentences.l:
Latona's silent breast the joys thrill:
such was Dido, such did she carry herself, glad,
through their midst, pressing on the work and the kingdoms to come.
sentences.i: joy thrills Latona's silent heart. Such was Dido, such was her glad bearing as she moved among them, urging on her work and the kingdom to come.
sentences.n: 'Latonae tacitum pertemptant gaudia pectus' — an interlaced order: genitive, adjective, verb, subject, noun, with 'tacitum ... pectus' enclosing the verb and its subject; 'tacitum' (silent) means that her joy is inward, without speech. 'talis ... talem' — 'such ... such': 'talem' agrees with 'se', 'such a one she showed herself'. 'instans operi regnisque futuris' — 'pressing on' (present participle of 'insto') with the dative, 'to the work and the kingdoms to come': Dido is already shown as a builder and ruler. The 'kingdoms to come' carry an irony: Carthage is the city fated to be Rome's enemy (I.12–22).

sentences.t:
Tum foribus divae, media testudine templi,
saepta armis, solioque alte subnixa resedit.
sentences.l:
Then at the doors of the goddess, in the middle of the temple's vault,
fenced with arms, and raised high on her throne, she sat down.
sentences.i: Then at the doors of the goddess, under the middle of the temple's vault, guarded by armed men and raised high on a throne, she took her seat.
sentences.n: 'foribus divae' — 'at the doors of the goddess' (Juno, whose temple it is). 'media testudine templi' — 'under the middle of the vault'; 'testudo' (tortoise) is also the word for a vault or arched roof. 'saepta armis' — 'hedged round with arms'; 'saepta' is the perfect passive participle of 'saepio'. 'solio alte subnixa' — 'resting high upon a throne': 'subnixa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'subnitor'. 'resedit' — 'she sat down', took her seat (from 'resido').

sentences.t:
Iura dabat legesque viris, operumque laborem
partibus aequabat iustis, aut sorte trahebat:
sentences.l:
She was giving judgments and laws to the men, and the labour of the works
she was making even in fair portions, or drawing by lot:
sentences.i: She gave judgments and laws to her people, and shared out the burden of the work in fair portions, or assigned it by lot:
sentences.n: 'Iura dabat legesque' — 'she was giving judgments and laws' (imperfects of the scene in progress): the first hints of the queen's civic authority. 'operum laborem' — the labour of the building works. 'partibus aequabat iustis' — 'made equal in just portions'. 'aut sorte trahebat' — 'or drew by lot', i.e. assigned by drawing lots. The colon prepares the sudden 'cum subito' that follows: an imperfect narrating the background, then a surprise ('cum' inversum — 'when suddenly').

sentences.t:
cum subito Aeneas concursu accedere magno
Anthea Sergestumque videt fortemque Cloanthum,
Teucrorumque alios, ater quos aequore turbo
dispulerat penitusque alias avexerat oras.
sentences.l:
when suddenly Aeneas sees, approaching in a great concourse,
Antheus and Sergestus and brave Cloanthus,
and others of the Teucrians, whom the black whirlwind on the sea
had scattered and carried far away to other shores.
sentences.i: when suddenly Aeneas sees Antheus, Sergestus and brave Cloanthus, with other Trojans whom the dark whirlwind had scattered over the sea and swept off to distant shores, coming up with a great crowd.
sentences.n: 'cum subito' — 'when suddenly': the cum-clause that carries the main event (the 'inverted cum' construction) after the imperfects of the preceding lines. 'concursu accedere magno' — 'approaching in a great crowd', with 'accedere' completing 'videt' (accusative and infinitive). Antheus (I.181), Sergestus and Cloanthus (I.222) were captains of ships lost in the storm; Sergestus and Cloanthus will later be named as ancestors of Roman families (V.121–123). 'Teucrorumque' — 'and of the Teucrians', the Trojans (from Teucer, an early king of Troy). 'ater turbo' — the black whirlwind of I.81 ff. 'dispulerat ... avexerat' — pluperfects of 'dispello' (perfect 'dispuli') and 'aveho' (perfect 'avexi'). 'penitus' — deep into, far away; 'alias ... oras' — 'to other shores', accusative of the goal without a preposition.

sentences.t:
Obstipuit simul ipse simul perculsus Achates
laetitiaque metuque;
sentences.l:
He was stunned at once himself, at once struck was Achates
with gladness and with fear;
sentences.i: Aeneas and Achates were stunned together, struck at once with gladness and with fear;
sentences.n: The simple double 'simul ... simul' — 'at the same time ... at the same time' — joins the two men. 'laetitiaque metuque' — ablative of cause, with '-que ... -que' (both ... and); it is the double '-que ... -que' construction you will see often: 'both gladness and fear'. 'perculsus' — struck (perfect participle of 'percello'). 'Obstipuit' — perfect of 'obstipesco': the ordinary effect of a sudden shock in Virgil: stunned into stillness.

sentences.t:
avidi coniungere dextras
ardebant;
sentences.l:
eager to join right hands
they were burning;
sentences.i: they were burning to clasp their hands in greeting;
sentences.n: 'avidi coniungere dextras ardebant' — 'eager to join right hands, they were burning': the infinitive 'coniungere' depends on 'avidi' (like 'cupidus' with an infinitive, a poetic extension). Joining right hands is the Roman gesture of greeting and pledge. 'coniungere' has four syllables, con-iun-ge-re: the 'i' after the prefix is a consonant (like English y).

sentences.t: sed res animos incognita turbat.
sentences.l: but the unknown matter disturbs their minds.
sentences.i: but the uncertainty of it all troubles their minds.
sentences.n: 'res incognita' — 'the unknown situation': they do not yet know the fate of the others, or what reception they will get. 'animos ... turbat' — 'confuses their minds'. The 'sed' makes the contrast with the eager right hands.

sentences.i: They hide their feelings and, wrapped in the hollow cloud, watch to see what has become of the men, on what shore they have left the fleet, and why they have come;
sentences.n: 'Dissimulant' — 'they conceal (their feelings)'. 'nube cava ... amicti' — 'clothed in the hollow cloud', the mist Venus gave them at I.411. 'quae fortuna viris, ... quo litore linquant, quid veniant' — three indirect questions with the subjunctive; 'quae fortuna viris' has no verb (supply 'sit'): 'what fortune (is) for the men'. 'linquant' — present subjunctive (primary sequence after the present 'speculantur'): on what shore they are leaving, that is have left, the fleet. 'quid veniant' — 'quid' here means 'why'. The indirect questions are as natural in Latin as they are heavy in English.

sentences.t:
cunctis nam lecti navibus ibant,
orantes veniam, et templum clamore petebant.
sentences.l:
for chosen men from all the ships were coming,
begging favour, and they sought the temple with a shout.
sentences.i: for picked men from every ship were coming to beg a kind hearing, and they made for the temple with a cry.
sentences.n: 'cunctis nam lecti navibus' — 'for (men) chosen from all the ships': 'nam', 'for', is put second in its clause, a poetic order. 'orantes veniam' — 'asking for favour'; 'venia' is indulgence, a kind hearing. 'clamore petebant' — 'sought with a shout': an imperfect, as the deputation advances; the shout is a plea.

sentences.t:
Postquam introgressi et coram data copia fandi,
maxumus Ilioneus placido sic pectore coepit:
sentences.l:
When they had gone in, and the chance of speaking was given in their presence,
the eldest Ilioneus began, in a calm heart, thus:
sentences.i: When they had entered and been given a chance to speak in her presence, Ilioneus, the eldest, began calmly with these words:
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'Postquam introgressi' (supply 'sunt') — 'after they had gone in': perfect of the deponent 'introgredior', with 'sunt' left out; 'et coram data copia fandi' (supply 'est') — 'and the opportunity of speaking face to face was given'. 'fandi' is the genitive of the gerund of 'for', 'I speak'. 'maxumus' — Greenough's spelling of 'maximus' (the superlative of 'magnus'; here 'eldest'). Ilioneus captained one of the ships in the storm (I.120) and will speak for the Trojans again before King Latinus (VII.212 ff.). 'placido pectore' — 'with a calm heart'. 'sic ... coepit' — the speech follows.

sentences.t:
“O Regina, novam cui condere Iuppiter urbem
iustitiaque dedit gentis frenare superbas,
sentences.l:
“O Queen, to whom Jupiter has given to found a new city
and to curb proud nations with justice,
sentences.i: “O Queen, to whom Jupiter has granted the founding of a new city and the bridling of proud nations by justice,
sentences.n: The speech of Ilioneus runs to I.558 (the closing mark is there). 'cui condere ... dedit ... frenare' — 'dare' with the infinitive, 'granted (her) to found' and 'to curb', a poetic construction; 'novam ... urbem' frames 'cui condere Iuppiter'. 'iustitia' is ablative of means: it is by justice, not force, that she is to rule. The courteous captatio benevolentiae comes first; the plea follows. 'gentis ... superbas' — accusative plural -is; compare Anchises' charge to Rome, 'debellare superbos' (VI.853).

sentences.t:
Troes te miseri, ventis maria omnia vecti,
oramus,
sentences.l:
We Trojans, wretched, carried by the winds over all seas,
beg you,
sentences.i: We, wretched Trojans, carried by the winds over every sea, beg you:
sentences.n: 'Troes te miseri' — the speakers put themselves first and the pronoun for the queen second; 'Troes' is a Greek nominative plural, two syllables (Tro-es); 'te' is the object of 'oramus'. 'ventis maria omnia vecti' — 'carried by the winds over all seas' (the perfect participle of 'veho' with the accusative of the space crossed: 'maria omnia'). The idea of the second half of the sentence follows in the next unit: 'prohibe ... parce ... aspice'.

sentences.t:
prohibe infandos a navibus ignis,
parce pio generi, et propius res aspice nostras.
sentences.l:
keep the unspeakable fires from the ships,
spare a pious race, and look more closely on our affairs.
sentences.i: keep terrible fire away from our ships, spare a god-fearing people, and look more closely at our case.
sentences.n: Three imperatives: 'prohibe', 'parce' (with the dative 'generi'), 'aspice'. 'infandos ... ignis' — 'unspeakable fires': the Libyans, it seems, had been threatening to burn the Trojan ships (compare 'bella cient' below). 'pio generi' — pius is Aeneas' word, the Trojan quality: 'dutiful to gods and kin'. 'propius' — 'more closely', 'with more attention'. 'res ... nostras' — 'our affairs', 'our situation'.

sentences.t:
Non nos aut ferro Libycos populare Penatis
venimus, aut raptas ad litora vertere praedas;
sentences.l:
Not to lay waste with the sword the Libyan household gods have we
come, nor to drive seized plunder to the shore;
sentences.i: We have not come to ravage the Libyan homes with the sword, or to drive stolen plunder down to the coast;
sentences.n: 'Non nos aut ferro ... venimus, aut ... ' — the Trojans deny two hostile purposes with the infinitive of purpose after a verb of motion ('populare', 'vertere'); 'populare' is the active form of the usually deponent 'populor'. 'Penatis' — the Penates, household gods, here used for 'homes' (a metonymy; and another Greenough accusative plural in -is). 'raptas ad litora vertere praedas' — 'to turn plunder, once seized, towards the shore' (the usual cattle-raiding image: to drive loot to the beach).

sentences.t: non ea vis animo, nec tanta superbia victis.
sentences.l: There is not that violence in our spirit, nor so great pride in the conquered.
sentences.i: We have no such violence in us, nor such pride in the beaten.
sentences.n: 'Non ea vis animo' — 'there is not that force for the mind' (dative of possession, supply 'est'). 'nec tanta superbia victis' — 'nor so great pride to the conquered' (the same dative; 'victis' = those conquered, the Trojans). Ilioneus speaks as a diplomat: a beaten people claims no pride.

sentences.t:
Est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt,
terra antiqua, potens armis atque ubere glaebae;
sentences.l:
There is a place, Greeks call it Hesperia by name,
an ancient land, mighty in arms and in the richness of its soil;
sentences.i: There is a region, Hesperia to the Greeks, an ancient land, powerful in arms and in the richness of its soil;
sentences.n: 'Est locus' — the formula of the introduction of a place, a favourite epic opening. 'Hesperiam ... cognomine' — 'by the name Hesperia' (Hesperia: 'western land', Italy, as seen from Greece); 'Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt' is set beside 'Est locus' without a relative ('which the Greeks call'). 'Grai' — the same word as 'Graii' (467), contracted to two syllables. 'potens armis atque ubere glaebae' — 'powerful in arms and in the fertility of the clod' ('ubere' is an ablative of the neuter noun 'uber', richness; 'glaebae' the genitive of the soil). These four lines (530–533) return word for word at III.163–166.

sentences.t:
Oenotri coluere viri; nunc fama minores
Italiam dixisse ducis de nomine gentem.
sentences.l:
Oenotrian men have farmed it; now rumour says, the later ones
have called the nation Italy, from the name of their leader.
sentences.i: Oenotrian men once farmed it; now, as the story goes, their descendants have called the nation Italy, after the name of a leader.
sentences.n: 'Oenotri' — the Oenotrians, an ancient people of southern Italy (named from a legendary king, Oenotrus). 'coluere' — for 'coluerunt' (the -ere = -erunt ending, which you will see constantly). 'fama' — 'the story is that'; 'minores' — 'those who came later', the descendants; the accusative and infinitive 'Italiam dixisse ... gentem' depends on 'fama' as if it were 'fama est'. 'ducis de nomine' — 'from the name of a leader': Italus.

sentences.t: Hic cursus fuit:
sentences.l: This was our course:
sentences.i: This was the course we held:
sentences.n: A half-line. 'Hic cursus fuit' — 'this was our course' ('hic' agrees with 'cursus'): five syllables, two and a half feet, then the line stops. Virgil left more than fifty such unfinished lines; the ancient Life of Virgil says he let some lines stand incomplete so as not to hold up the work, and the poem was unrevised when he died. The sentence goes on with 'cum subito' in the next line.

sentences.t:
cum subito adsurgens fluctu nimbosus Orion
in vada caeca tulit, penitusque procacibus austris
perque undas, superante salo, perque invia saxa
dispulit; huc pauci vestris adnavimus oris.
sentences.l:
when suddenly rising from the wave, rainy Orion
bore us into hidden shallows, and far and wide with bold south winds,
and through the waves, the sea overwhelming, and through pathless rocks
scattered us; hither we few have swum to your shores.
sentences.i: when suddenly Orion rose out of the waves in a storm of rain and swept us into hidden shoals, and with the wild south winds drove us far and wide, through the waves, with the sea flooding over us, and through rocks where no path lies; and we, a few, have swum here to your shores.
sentences.n: 'cum subito' again (the 'inverted cum'). 'Orion' — the constellation whose rising and setting brought storms; here three syllables with a short O, O-ri-on; 'nimbosus' — rain-bringing; 'adsurgens fluctu' — rising out of the wave. 'in vada caeca tulit' — 'bore us into blind shallows' (unseen reefs). 'penitusque ... dispulit' — and 'scattered us far in' — with 'procacibus austris' (ablative, 'bold south winds'), 'superante salo' (ablative absolute, 'the brine overpowering'), and 'perque ... perque' (both ... and). 'huc pauci vestris adnavimus oris' — 'we few have swum here to your shores' — 'adnavimus' a compound of 'nare' (swim), with the dative of direction ('oris'). 'dispulit' has the Trojans as its object understood.

sentences.t: Quod genus hoc hominum?
sentences.l: What race of men is this?
sentences.i: What kind of people is this?
sentences.n: 'Quod genus hoc hominum?' — 'what sort of men is this?' It is a bitter, indignant cry, not a question for an answer.

sentences.t:
Quaeve hunc tam barbara morem
permittit patria?
sentences.l:
Or what so barbarous fatherland this custom
permits?
sentences.i: What country is so barbarous as to allow such a custom?
sentences.n: 'Quaeve hunc tam barbara morem permittit patria?' — 'or what country so barbarous allows this custom?': 'quae' (what), '-ve' (or), 'hunc ... morem' (this custom), 'patria' (nominative, the subject). 'tam barbara' agrees with 'patria', 'what country so barbarous': the word-order 'hunc tam barbara morem' interlocks the nouns and adjectives.

sentences.t: Hospitio prohibemur harenae;
sentences.l: We are shut out from the hospitality of the sand;
sentences.i: We are kept from the welcome even of the beach;
sentences.n: 'Hospitio prohibemur harenae' — the bitter complaint: 'we are barred from the hospitality of the sand'. 'harenae' is a genitive of 'harena', the beach; 'hospitio' is ablative of separation, 'from'. The Trojans are not even allowed to land.

sentences.t: bella cient, primaque vetant consistere terra.
sentences.l: they stir up wars, and forbid us to stand on the first land.
sentences.i: They stir up war, and forbid us to set foot on the nearest land.
sentences.n: 'bella cient' — 'they rouse wars' (from 'cieo', 'to stir'). 'primaque vetant consistere terra' — 'and forbid (us) to stand on the first earth' — i.e. the land at the water's edge; 'prima terra' is ablative of place where. A brusque, hard line, as the speaker feels it.

sentences.t:
Si genus humanum et mortalia temnitis arma
at sperate deos memores fandi atque nefandi.
sentences.l:
If you despise the human race and mortal arms
yet expect gods mindful of right and wrong.
sentences.i: If you scorn the human race and the weapons of men, yet look to gods who remember right and wrong.
sentences.n: Greenough's text has no comma after 'arma' where the sense calls for one: 'si ... temnitis arma, / at sperate'. The 'si ... at' is the usual structure of a plea ('if not ..., at least ...'). 'temnitis' — 'you despise' ('temno', the poets' word for 'contemno'). 'sperate' — here 'expect', 'look for', not 'hope'. 'genus humanum et mortalia ... arma' — 'the human race and mortal arms' (the arms of men). 'deos memores fandi atque nefandi' — 'gods mindful of what may be spoken and what may not' — i.e. mindful of right and wrong ('fandi atque nefandi' are genitives with 'memores' of 'fandum' and 'nefandum', gerundive forms used as nouns). The threat is gentle: the gods will remember.

sentences.t:
Rex erat Aeneas nobis, quo iustior alter,
nec pietate fuit, nec bello maior et armis.
sentences.l:
A king we had, Aeneas, than whom no other more just
was in piety, nor greater in war and arms.
sentences.i: We had a king, Aeneas: no one was more just in his piety than he, nor greater in war and arms.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Rex erat Aeneas nobis' — 'there was to us a king, Aeneas' (dative of possession). 'quo iustior alter / nec pietate fuit, nec bello maior et armis' — 'than whom no other was juster in piety, nor greater in war and arms': 'quo' is the ablative of comparison with both comparatives, 'iustior' and 'maior'; 'nec ... nec' does the negating; 'pietate', 'bello', 'armis' are ablatives of respect. Ilioneus speaks of Aeneas in the past tense without knowing he is standing there, hidden in the cloud. 'pietas', on his own men's lips here, is the central quality of the whole poem.

sentences.i: If the fates are keeping him safe, if he still feeds on the air of heaven and does not yet lie in the cruel shadows, there is no cause for fear;
sentences.n: 'Quem si fata virum servant' — 'and if the fates preserve this man': 'quem ... virum' is a connecting relative used as an adjective with 'virum', and comes first in the sentence. 'vescitur aura aetheria' — 'feeds upon the ethereal air' (he is alive: 'vescor' takes the ablative). 'neque adhuc ... occubat' — 'and does not yet lie in death'. 'non metus' — 'no fear' (supply 'est'); the clause is left open until the next line: 'officio nec te certasse priorem paeniteat'.

sentences.t:
officio nec te certasse priorem
paeniteat.
sentences.l:
nor that in kindness you vied first
should you regret.
sentences.i: nor should you regret having been the first to vie in kindness.
sentences.n: 'officio nec te certasse priorem paeniteat' — 'nor should you regret having contended first in kindness': 'paeniteat' is the present subjunctive of the impersonal verb 'paenitet', which takes the accusative of the person ('te'); 'certasse' is the contracted perfect infinitive for 'certavisse'; 'officio' is ablative, 'in kindness, in service'. 'priorem' agrees with 'te': you would be the first. A promise that kindness to Aeneas will be repaid.

sentences.t:
Sunt et Siculis regionibus urbes
arvaque, Troianoque a sanguine clarus Acestes.
sentences.l:
There are cities also in the Sicilian regions,
and fields, and Acestes, illustrious, of Trojan blood.
sentences.i: There are cities also in Sicily, and fields, and Acestes, a king of illustrious Trojan blood.
sentences.n: 'Sunt et Siculis regionibus urbes arvaque' — 'there are also in the Sicilian regions cities and fields', 'Siculis regionibus' being the ablative of place. Where Greenough has 'arvaque' ('and fields'), The Latin Library prints 'armaque' ('and arms'), which would change the sense; Greenough's reading is followed. 'Troianoque a sanguine clarus Acestes' — 'and Acestes, illustrious, of Trojan blood': a Sicilian king born of a Trojan mother, who had already given the Trojans wine at their departure (I.195–196); they return to him in Book V.

sentences.t:
Quassatam ventis liceat subducere classem,
et silvis aptare trabes et stringere remos:
sentences.l:
Let it be allowed to haul up the fleet, shattered by the winds,
and in the woods fit timbers and trim oars:
sentences.i: Let us be allowed to haul up our storm-battered fleet, to shape timbers in the woods and trim branches for oars:
sentences.n: 'liceat subducere' — 'let it be permitted to draw up (on the shore)' — an impersonal jussive of 'licet', with the infinitive. 'Quassatam ventis ... classem' — 'the fleet, shaken by winds', with the participle 'quassatam' (from 'quasso'). 'silvis aptare trabes' — 'to fit timbers in the woods' ('silvis' ablative of place), that is shape new planks; 'stringere remos' — 'to strip/trim oars', that is to dress the oars for use. The colon begins the exposition of the two alternatives.

sentences.t:
si datur Italiam, sociis et rege recepto,
tendere, ut Italiam laeti Latiumque petamus;
sentences.l:
if it is granted to Italy, our companions and king recovered,
to make our way, so that joyfully we may seek Italy and Latium;
sentences.i: if we may sail to Italy, with our comrades and our king restored, that we may joyfully seek Italy and Latium;
sentences.n: 'si datur Italiam ... tendere' — 'if it is granted to head for Italy' (the infinitive after 'datur'). 'sociis et rege recepto' — an ablative absolute: 'our comrades and our king having been recovered' (the singular participle 'recepto' agrees with the nearest noun, 'rege'). 'ut ... petamus' — a purpose clause: 'so that we may seek'. The men know their goal: Aeneas told them 'tendimus in Latium' (I.205).

sentences.t:
sin absumpta salus, et te, pater optume Teucrum,
pontus habet Lybiae, nec spes iam restat Iuli,
at freta Sicaniae saltem sedesque paratas,
unde huc advecti, regemque petamus Acesten.”
sentences.l:
but if safety is gone, and you, best father of the Teucrians,
the sea of Libya holds, and no hope now remains of Iulus,
at least the Sicilian straits and the seats prepared,
whence we were carried here, and King Acestes, let us seek.”
sentences.i: But if our safety is lost and the Libyan sea has you, best father of the Trojans, and there is no hope now left of Iulus, then let us at least make for the Sicilian waters and the homes prepared for us there, from which we came here, and for King Acestes.”
sentences.n: 'sin absumpta salus' — 'but if safety has been used up' (supply 'est'); 'et te, pater optume Teucrum, pontus habet Lybiae' — 'and you, best father of the Teucrians, the Libyan sea holds': the vocative 'pater optume' is addressed to Aeneas, not Dido (it is spoken as if he were lost); 'Teucrum' is an old genitive plural (-um for -orum); 'optume' and 'Lybiae' are Greenough's spellings of 'optime' and 'Libyae'. 'nec spes iam restat Iuli' — Iulus is Aeneas' son, Ascanius (I.267); 'Iuli' has three syllables, I-u-li. 'at freta Sicaniae saltem sedesque paratas ... regemque petamus Acesten' — 'at least let us seek the straits of Sicania (Sicily) and the seats prepared, whence we were carried here, and King Acestes' — in 'unde huc advecti' supply 'sumus'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: Talibus Ilioneus;
sentences.l: With such words Ilioneus;
sentences.i: So spoke Ilioneus;
sentences.n: 'Talibus Ilioneus' — the standard formula after a speech, with the verb of speaking missing ('Talibus ... dixit' understood): the same ellipsis of the verb of speaking as in 'haec secum' and 'Aeolus haec contra' in the earlier parts. The semicolon joins it to the reaction of the others in the next line.

sentences.t:
cuncti simul ore fremebant
Dardanidae.
sentences.l:
all together murmured with their mouths
the Dardanids.
sentences.i: and all the sons of Dardanus murmured their assent together.
sentences.n: 'cuncti simul ore fremebant Dardanidae' — 'all together the Dardanidae murmured with their mouths' — 'ore' is an ablative of means, and 'Dardanidae' is the nominative plural of the Greek patronymic ('sons of Dardanus', that is the Trojans); the word stands alone as a half-line, another of the unfinished lines (compare 534). The sentence is finished, and the next part resumes with Dido's answer (I.561).
